comments.author: @pedrogorilla483
comments.text:
A few more critiques about the proposed New Turing Test:

$100K to $1M is such an arbitrary sum of money to qualify such an incredible advancement. What difference would it make if it was $50K to $500K?

Also, $100K is a ludicrous amount of money to experiment with, it prohibits the vast majority of people from even starting. 

I also think a 10x return  not enough to prove autonomous agency. It can be achieved through luck, influence, and other means that are not reproducible. 

A more appropriate measure in my opinion would be focused on the ROI regardless of the starting sum, as well as the means through which the goals were achieved rather than the pure amount of money it ended up with. 

I think this would require either very specific training or more complex set of instructions, and human supervision because there are many illegal and unethical ways to turn $100K into $1M that would be achievable by an autonomous agent coldly trying to achieve that.

comments.author: @nuclearthrone2497
comments.text:
Video Summary:

In this video, Wes Roth explores the concept of autonomous AI agents capable of generating income and potentially passing the modern Turing test. This test, proposed by Mustafa Suleiman, involves an AI making one million dollars on a retail web platform within a few months with just a $100,000 starting investment.

Wes discusses the advancements in AI, particularly focusing on OpenAI's GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 Turbo. GPT-4, a more intelligent but slower and more expensive model, can create tools for faster, cheaper models like GPT-3.5 Turbo. With these tools, the lightweight model can perform tasks at the same level as GPT-4, indicating that autonomous AI agents capable of generating income may not be too far off.

The video then delves into the research conducted by Nvidia, Google DeepMind, Stanford, and Microsoft. Nvidia's "Voyager AI Minecraft Agent" operates in the world of Minecraft, aiming to become the best Minecraft player. The agent, controlled by GPT-4, decides what to do based on a broad objective and codes different skills to use, tests them, and saves them for later if they work well.

Google and Stanford's "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior" study created 25 agents, each powered by its own GPT-4, that live in a virtual village. Each agent has a backstory, daily activities, and relationships with other agents. They go about their day, make plans, and interact with each other in a believable manner.

These studies indicate that we might be closer to AI agents capable of making a million dollars with minimal input than previously thought. However, there are still some challenges to overcome. One important aspect is giving AI agents vision, enabling them to see and interact with websites and the broader internet effectively.

Andrej Karpathy, a main developer at OpenAI, believes that AGI will take the form of some kind of AI agent and that the people building AI agents are at the forefront of AI capability. He suggests that the big labs are not at the edge of capability, but the entrepreneurs and hackers are.

John Carmack, a key figure in the video game industry, believes that the code for artificial general intelligence (AGI) could be written by a single individual and could be tens of thousands of lines of code, not millions. He suggests that there are probably less than six key insights that need to be made to achieve AGI.

The video concludes by suggesting that the development of autonomous AI agents capable of generating income is closer than we might think, and it could potentially be achieved by a single individual or a small team.
